docs.title: Module 0 - How code runs
docs.text:
Back to Home

Objective: run a short program, make it print what you want, and fix it when it breaks.

Time: about 1 hour, over two sessions.

Lesson What you learn 0.1 Your first program print, text vs. numbers, running top to bottom, comments 0.2 Reading error messages The three errors you'll hit most, and how to read them Checkpoint 0 Prove it: no hints

Optional reading, for a second angle: CS50P Lecture 0 at cs50.harvard.edu/python, and the Python basics chapter of Automate the Boring Stuff at automatetheboringstuff.com.

docs.title: 0.1 Your first program
docs.text: Module 0 · about 25 minutes

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
A program is a list of instructions that Python carries out one line at a time, top to bottom. Think of a model where every cell is computed in a fixed order: line 1, then line 2, then line 3. Nothing runs out of order, and nothing runs twice unless you tell it to.

print(...) is the instruction that shows something on screen. Whatever goes inside the parentheses gets displayed.

  • Text goes inside quotes: print("Hello"). Text in quotes is called a string.
  • Numbers go without quotes, and Python does the math first: print(2 + 3) shows 5.
  • Several items can go in one print, separated by commas. Python puts a space between them: print("Price:", 120.5) shows Price: 120.5.
  • A comment starts with #. Python ignores everything after the # on that line. Use comments to leave notes, or to switch a line off without deleting it.

One trap to watch for: print("2 + 3") shows the text 2 + 3, because the quotes make it a string. Quotes mean "show this exactly as written."

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
Press Run. Then change the numbers or the text and run it again.

kind: example
id: ex-0-1
title: print in action
--- starter
# Lines starting with # are comments. Python skips them.
print("Hello from Python")
print(2 + 3)
print("2 + 3")
print("Revenue ($m):", 1250)
print("Next year at 8% growth:", 1250 * 1.08)

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
1. Make the program print exactly Hello, Python, with a capital H, a comma, and a capital P.

id: m0-hello
title: Hello, Python
--- starter
print("")
--- tests
lines = output.strip().splitlines()
check(len(lines) == 1, "print exactly one line")
check(lines and lines[0] == "Hello, Python", f"the line should read 'Hello, Python' (yours: {lines[0] if lines else 'nothing'})")
--- hint
Put the text between the two quote marks.
--- hint
Capitals, the comma and the space all count. The text must match exactly.
--- solution
print("Hello, Python")

2. Print two lines. The first is Ticker: ACME. The second is Price: 120.5, where 120.5 is a number, not text.

id: m0-two-lines
title: Two lines
--- starter
# Line 1: the ticker


# Line 2: the price, using a comma and a number

--- tests
lines = output.strip().splitlines()
check(len(lines) == 2, f"print exactly two lines (you printed {len(lines)})")
check(len(lines) > 0 and lines[0] == "Ticker: ACME", "line 1 should be 'Ticker: ACME'")
check(len(lines) > 1 and lines[1] == "Price: 120.5", "line 2 should be 'Price: 120.5'")
check("120.5)" in code.replace(" ", ""), "pass 120.5 as a number after a comma, like print(\"Price:\", 120.5)")
--- hint
Each print makes one line, so you need two prints.
--- hint
For line 2, put the label in quotes, then a comma, then the number without quotes.
--- solution

print("Price:", 120.5)

3. A $1,000 deposit earns 5% for one year. Have Python calculate the ending balance, deposit × (1 + rate), and print it. Don't type the answer yourself.

id: m0-math-print
title: Let Python do the math
--- starter
print()
--- tests
check(output.strip() == "1050.0", f"Python should print 1050.0 (yours: {output.strip() or 'nothing'})")
check("*" in code, "use * for multiplication, so Python does the calculation")
--- hint
Multiplication in Python is `*`. Growing by 5% means multiplying by 1.05.
--- solution
print(1000 * 1.05)

4. These deal steps print in the wrong order. Rearrange the lines so they print 1, 2, 3, 4. Copy and paste is fine.

id: m0-order
title: Deal steps in order
--- starter
print("3. Submit IOI")
print("1. Sign NDA")
print("4. Management meeting")
print("2. Receive CIM")
--- tests
lines = output.strip().splitlines()
check(lines == ["1. Sign NDA", "2. Receive CIM", "3. Submit IOI", "4. Management meeting"],
      "the four steps should print in order 1, 2, 3, 4")
--- hint
Python runs lines top to bottom, so the top line prints first.
--- solution
print("1. Sign NDA")
print("2. Receive CIM")
print("3. Submit IOI")
print("4. Management meeting")

5. Switch off the middle line with a comment, so the program prints only the first and last lines. Don't delete it.

id: m0-comment
title: Comment it out
--- starter
print("Base case: 12% IRR")
print("Draft number - do not show")
print("Downside case: 7% IRR")
--- tests
lines = output.strip().splitlines()
check(lines == ["Base case: 12% IRR", "Downside case: 7% IRR"], "only the base case and downside case lines should print")
check("Draft number" in code, "keep the middle line in your code; comment it out instead of deleting it")
--- hint
Put `#` at the very start of the line you want to switch off.
--- solution
print("Base case: 12% IRR")
# print("Draft number - do not show")
print("Downside case: 7% IRR")

docs.title: Explain it back
docs.text:
In your own words: what's the difference between print(1000 * 1.05) and print("1000 * 1.05")?

Model answer

The first has no quotes, so Python calculates the expression and prints 1050.0. The second is a string because of the quotes, so Python prints the characters exactly as written: 1000 * 1.05.

Next: 0.2 Reading error messages

docs.title: 0.2 Reading error messages
docs.text: Module 0 · about 25 minutes

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
Errors are normal. Professional programmers hit them all day. An error message is Python telling you what went wrong and where, the same way Excel shows #NAME? or #VALUE! in the broken cell.

On this site an error looks like Line 2: NameError: name 'prnt' is not defined. Read it in three parts:

  1. Line 2 is where to look.
  2. NameError is the kind of problem.
  3. name 'prnt' is not defined is the detail.

These are the three errors you'll hit most:

Error Plain English Excel cousin Usual cause SyntaxError "I can't even read this line" A formula with a missing bracket Missing ) or a missing quote mark NameError "I don't know that word" #NAME? A typo (prnt), or text missing its quotes TypeError "Those two things don't mix" #VALUE! Adding text to a number with +

One habit to build now: when something breaks, read the error before you touch the code.

docs.text:
Run this as is and read the error. Then fix the typo and run it again.

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
Each program below is broken. Run it first, read the error, then fix it.

1. Missing piece.

id: m0-fix-syntax
title: Fix the SyntaxError
--- starter
print("Revenue grew 12% this year"
--- tests
check(output.strip() == "Revenue grew 12% this year", "the program should print: Revenue grew 12% this year")
--- hint
Every opening bracket needs a closing one.
--- solution

2. Python doesn't recognize a word.

id: m0-fix-name
title: Fix the NameError (typo)
--- starter
print("Sponsor: Sycamore")
Print("Facility: First-lien term loan")
--- tests

check(lines == ["Sponsor: Sycamore", "Facility: First-lien term loan"], "both lines should print")
--- hint
Python is case-sensitive. `print` and `Print` are different words.
--- solution

3. This one should print the word Covenant, but Python thinks it's a name.

id: m0-fix-quotes
title: Fix the NameError (missing quotes)
--- starter
print(Covenant)
--- tests
check(output.strip() == "Covenant", "the program should print: Covenant")
--- hint
Text needs quote marks around it. Without them, Python looks for something named Covenant.
--- solution

4. Text and a number don't mix with +. Make it print Leverage: 5.2x using commas inside print. Keep 5.2 as a number.

id: m0-fix-type
title: Fix the TypeError
--- starter
print("Leverage: " + 5.2 + "x")
--- tests
check(output.strip() in ("Leverage: 5.2 x", "Leverage: 5.2x"), f"should print 'Leverage: 5.2 x' or 'Leverage: 5.2x' (yours: {output.strip()})")

--- hint
Replace each `+` with a comma. Commas let print mix text and numbers.
--- hint
Commas add a space, so you'll get `Leverage: 5.2 x`. That's fine for now. Module 1 shows how to remove the space.
--- solution
print("Leverage:", 5.2, "x")

--- tests

check(lines == ["Deal: Project Arrow", "Size ($m): 235", "Tenor (years): 7"], "all three lines should print correctly")
--- hint
Line 1 is missing something at the end of the text.
--- hint
Line 3 is missing the separator between the label and the number.
--- solution
print("Deal: Project Arrow")
print("Size ($m):", 235)
print("Tenor (years):", 7)

docs.title: Explain it back
docs.text:
You see Line 3: NameError: name 'revnue' is not defined. What's wrong, and where would you look?

Model answer

Look at line 3. Python found a word it doesn't recognize: revnue, almost certainly a typo for revenue. Either fix the spelling, or, if it was meant to be text, put it in quotes.

Lesson What you learn 1.1 Numbers and arithmetic Math operators, order of operations, the Excel ^ trap, rounding 1.2 Variables Naming values, reusing them, updating them 1.3 Text and formatting Strings, f-strings, money and percent formats, converting types 1.4 True and False Comparisons, and / or / not, covenant-style tests 1.5 Capstone - loan payment Put it together: a mortgage and a term loan Checkpoint 1 Prove it: a bond price and a terminal value, no hints

docs.title: 1.1 Numbers and arithmetic
docs.text: Module 1 · about 30 minutes

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
Python is a calculator that follows the same order of operations as Excel: parentheses first, then powers, then multiplication and division, then addition and subtraction.

Operation Python Example Result Add, subtract + - 900 - 150 750 Multiply, divide * / 1250 * 0.25 312.5 Power ** 1.05 ** 10 1.6288... Whole-number division // 25000 // 173 144 Remainder % 25000 % 173 88 Round round(x, 2) round(1628.894, 2) 1628.89

The Excel trap: in Excel, ^ means power. In Python, power is **. ^ means something else entirely, and with decimal numbers it raises a TypeError.

Python has two kinds of numbers. Integers (int) are whole numbers, like 1250. Floats (float) have a decimal point, like 0.25. Dividing with / always gives a float, so 10 / 2 is 5.0.

Floats are occasionally off in the last decimal place: 0.1 + 0.2 gives 0.30000000000000004. Excel has the same quirk and hides it. In Python, use round() when you display results.

docs.text:
kind: example
id: ex-1-1
title: Python as a calculator
--- starter
print(1250 * 0.25)
print(1.05 ** 10)            # compound growth factor over 10 years
print(round(1.05 ** 10, 4))
print(25000 // 173, 25000 % 173)
print(0.1 + 0.2)
print(round(0.1 + 0.2, 2))

docs.text:
1. $1,000 compounds at 5% a year for 10 years. Print the ending value, starting amount × (1 + rate)^years, rounded to 2 decimals.

id: m1-compound
title: Compound growth
--- starter
print()
--- tests
check(output.strip() == "1628.89", f"should print 1628.89 (yours: {output.strip() or 'nothing'})")
check("**" in code, "use ** for the power")
--- hint
Python's power operator is `**`, so 1.05 to the power 10 is `1.05 ** 10`.
--- hint
Wrap the whole calculation in round(..., 2).
--- solution
print(round(1000 * 1.05 ** 10, 2))

2. A loan quotes 12% compounded monthly. Print the effective annual rate, (1 + 0.12/12)^12 - 1, rounded to 4 decimals.

id: m1-ear
title: Effective annual rate
--- starter
print()
--- tests
check(output.strip() == "0.1268", f"should print 0.1268 (yours: {output.strip() or 'nothing'})")
--- hint
Parentheses matter: (1 + 0.12 / 12) ** 12 - 1. Division happens before addition inside the parentheses, which is what you want.
--- solution

3. You have $25,000 to buy a stock at $173 a share. Print, on one line, how many whole shares you can buy and how much cash is left over.

id: m1-shares
title: Whole shares and leftover cash
--- starter
print()
--- tests
check(output.strip() == "144 88", f"should print '144 88' (yours: {output.strip() or 'nothing'})")
check("//" in code and "%" in code, "use // for whole shares and % for the remainder")
--- hint
`//` gives the whole number of times 173 fits into 25000. `%` gives what's left.
--- hint

--- solution

4. Someone pasted an Excel formula into Python. Fix it so it prints the 5-year growth factor at 8%, rounded to 4 decimals.

id: m1-excel-trap
title: The Excel ^ trap
--- starter

--- tests
check(output.strip() == "1.4693", f"should print 1.4693 (yours: {output.strip() or 'nothing'})")
--- hint
Python's power operator is two asterisks.
--- solution
print(round(1.08 ** 5, 4))

5. A 3-year bond pays a $5 coupon each year and $100 face value at maturity. The yield is 6%. Print its price, rounded to 3 decimals: each cash flow divided by 1.06 to the power of its year, all added up.

id: m1-bond-price
title: Price a bond by hand
--- starter
print()
--- tests
check(output.strip() == "97.327", f"should print 97.327 (yours: {output.strip() or 'nothing'})")
--- hint
Year 1: 5 / 1.06. Year 2: 5 / 1.06 ** 2. Year 3: (5 + 100) / 1.06 ** 3.
--- hint
Add the three pieces inside round(..., 3).
--- solution
print(round(5 / 1.06 + 5 / 1.06 ** 2 + 105 / 1.06 ** 3, 3))

docs.title: Explain it back
docs.text:
Why does 1.08 ^ 5 fail in Python, and what does 2 + 3 * 4 give?

Model answer

^ isn't Python's power operator. Power is **, and ^ doesn't work on decimal numbers, so Python raises a TypeError. 2 + 3 * 4 is 14, because multiplication happens before addition, the same as in Excel.

Next: 1.2 Variables

docs.title: 1.2 Variables
docs.text: Module 1 · about 30 minutes

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
A variable is a name for a value, like a named cell in Excel. Instead of re-typing 0.06 everywhere, you write rate = 0.06 once and use rate from then on.

principal = 10000
rate = 0.06
fv = principal * (1 + rate) ** 8

Read = as "store the result in," not "equals." Python works out the right-hand side first, then stores it under the name on the left. That's why this line works:

debt = debt - 100   # take the current debt, subtract 100, store it back as debt

Naming rules: use lowercase words joined by underscores (net_debt, max_leverage). No spaces, and a name can't start with a number. Names are case-sensitive, so Debt and debt are two different variables. Pick names a colleague could read without asking you.

A variable only updates when you assign to it. If you change rate after calculating fv, fv keeps its old value, unlike Excel, where formulas recalculate on their own. Code runs top to bottom, once.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
kind: example
id: ex-1-2
title: Variables in action
--- starter
debt = 450
ebitda = 90
leverage = debt / ebitda
print("Leverage:", leverage)

debt = debt - 100        # $100m paydown
print("Debt after paydown:", debt)
print("Leverage variable still says:", leverage)   # not recalculated
leverage = debt / ebitda
print("Recalculated leverage:", round(leverage, 2))

docs.title: Explain it back
docs.text:
You set rate = 0.06, calculate fv, then change rate = 0.07. What is fv now, and why is this different from Excel?

Model answer

fv still holds the value calculated at 6%. Python ran the fv line once, when it reached it, and doesn't recalculate it later. Excel recalculates formulas whenever an input changes. To get the 7% answer in Python, run the fv line again after changing rate.

docs.title: 1.3 Text and formatting
docs.text: Module 1 · about 35 minutes

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
A string is text in quotes. You'll use strings constantly for labels, tickers and report lines.

f-strings are the easiest way to put numbers inside text. Put f before the opening quote and put variables in curly braces:

company = "Cedar Corp"
ev = 1834.5
print(f"{company} EV: ${ev}m")      # Cedar Corp EV: $1834.5m

Add a format code after a colon inside the braces to control how a number looks. These work like Excel's number formats:

Format code Means {x:...} with x = 1234567.891 Excel equivalent ,.2f Comma separators, 2 decimals 1,234,567.89 #,##0.00 ,.0f Comma separators, no decimals 1,234,568 #,##0 .1% Percent, 1 decimal (multiplies by 100) use x = 0.2537 to get 25.4% 0.0%

Useful string tools:

  • .upper() and .lower() change case: "acme".upper() gives "ACME".
  • .strip() removes spaces from both ends: " ACME ".strip() gives "ACME". Messy data is full of stray spaces.
  • len("ACME") gives 4, the number of characters.

Converting types fixes the TypeError from 0.2. Data often arrives as text, even when it looks like a number.

  • float("173.25") turns text into a number you can do math with.
  • str(5.2) turns a number into text.

docs.title: Explain it back
docs.text:
Why does "173.25" * 40 not give 6930, and how do you fix it?

Model answer

"173.25" is text, not a number, because of the quotes. Multiplying text by 40 repeats the text 40 times. Convert it first with float("173.25"), then multiply.

Next: 1.4 True and False

docs.title: 1.4 True and False
docs.text: Module 1 · about 30 minutes

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
A comparison asks a yes/no question and gets back True or False, like Excel's =A1>5 returning TRUE. These two values are called booleans (type bool).

Question Python Watch out Greater / less than > < At least / at most >= <= Equal to == Two equals signs. A single = stores a value, it doesn't compare Not equal to !=

Combine questions with plain English words:

  • and: both must be true (dscr >= 1.25 and leverage <= 4.5)
  • or: at least one must be true (leverage > 6 or dscr < 1.1)
  • not: flips the answer (not in_default)

You can store the answer in a variable, which is exactly how a covenant test works: breach = leverage > max_leverage. In Module 2 you'll use these answers to make the program take different paths with if.

Text comparisons are exact: "acme" == "ACME" is False. Clean text before you compare it, using last lesson's .strip() and .upper().

Next: 1.5 Capstone - loan payment

docs.title: 1.5 Capstone - loan payment
docs.text: Module 1 · about 35 minutes

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
Nothing new in this lesson. You'll combine numbers, variables, formatting and comparisons into two small models. This is the habit to build: inputs at the top, calculations in the middle, output at the bottom, the same layout as a clean Excel model.

The level payment on an amortizing loan is the annuity formula:

payment = P * r / (1 - (1 + r) ** -n)

Here P is the principal, r is the rate per period, and n is the number of periods. For monthly payments, r = annual rate / 12 and n = years × 12. In Python, (1 + r)^(-n) is (1 + r) ** -n.

docs.title: Explain it back
docs.text:
Why do you divide the annual rate by 12 and multiply the years by 12 for monthly payments? What goes wrong if you only do one?

Model answer

The rate and the number of periods have to use the same unit of time. If you divide only the rate, you're pretending the loan lasts 30 months. If you multiply only the years, you're charging a full year's interest every month. Either way the payment comes out badly wrong.

docs.title: Checkpoint 1
docs.text:
Module 1 · about 20 minutes

No hints, and the solution unlocks only after you pass. Inputs at the top, calculations in the middle, output at the bottom.

1. Bond price. A 4-year bond with $1,000 face value pays a 4.5% annual coupon. The yield to maturity is 5.2%. Create:

  • price: the present value of all four years of cash flows. Each year pays a coupon of face × coupon rate, and year 4 also repays the face value. Divide each year's cash flow by (1 + ytm)^year and add them up.
  • is_discount: True if the bond trades below face value
  • label: exactly Price: $975.29 (discount). Build it with an f-string from price. You may type the word "discount."
id: m1-cp-bond
title: Bond price, discount flag, label
checkpoint: yes
--- starter
face = 1000
coupon_rate = 0.045
years = 4
ytm = 0.052

--- tests
check(approx(price, 975.29), f"price should be about 975.29 (yours: {price})")
check(is_discount is True, f"is_discount should be True (yours: {is_discount})")
check("<" in code or ">" in code, "calculate is_discount with a comparison")
check(label == "Price: $975.29 (discount)", f"label should be 'Price: $975.29 (discount)' (yours: '{label}')")
check("975" not in code, "let Python calculate the price; don't type it")
--- solution
face = 1000
coupon_rate = 0.045
years = 4
ytm = 0.052

coupon = face * coupon_rate
price = (coupon / (1 + ytm)
         + coupon / (1 + ytm) ** 2
         + coupon / (1 + ytm) ** 3
         + (coupon + face) / (1 + ytm) ** 4)
is_discount = price < face
label = f"Price: ${price:,.2f} (discount)"

2. Terminal value. Next year's free cash flow is $120m, the WACC is 9%, and the perpetual growth rate is 2.5%. Create terminal_value with the Gordon growth formula, FCF / (WACC - g). Also create sane, which is True only if WACC is greater than g and the terminal value is positive.

id: m1-cp-tv
title: Terminal value with a sanity check
checkpoint: yes
--- starter
fcf_next = 120
wacc = 0.09
g = 0.025

--- tests

check(sane is True, f"sane should be True (yours: {sane})")
check("and" in code, "combine both conditions in sane with and")
--- solution
fcf_next = 120
wacc = 0.09
g = 0.025

terminal_value = fcf_next / (wacc - g)
sane = wacc > g and terminal_value > 0

Pass both and Module 1 is done. The Home page should show it as Mastered. Module 2 (functions and conditionals) is next. It turns these calculations into reusable tools, such as a covenant_test() you can run on any borrower.

docs.title: 2.1 Making decisions
docs.text: Module 2 · about 35 minutes

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
In Module 1 you calculated breach = leverage > max_leverage, which gives True or False. Now you'll make the program do different things depending on that answer. It's Excel's IF, written as a block:

if leverage > max_leverage:
    status = "BREACH"
else:
    status = "PASS"
  • The line starts with if, then a condition, then a colon.
  • The lines that belong to the if are indented 4 spaces (press Tab). Python uses the indentation to know where the block ends. Indentation isn't decoration here, it's how Python reads the code. Get it wrong and you'll see a new error: IndentationError.
  • else: catches everything the if didn't.

For more than two outcomes, add elif ("else if"). It works like a nested IF in Excel:

if leverage <= 3.0:
    bucket = "Low"
elif leverage <= 5.0:
    bucket = "Moderate"
else:
    bucket = "High"

Python checks the conditions top to bottom and stops at the first true one. So order matters: put the narrowest test first. If leverage <= 5.0 came first, a 2.0x credit would land in "Moderate" and never reach "Low."

One new tool: abs(x) gives the size of a number without its sign. abs(-0.034) is 0.034.

From here on, keep the input lines exactly as given. The tests change those inputs (say, leverage = 5.6 becomes leverage = 3.0) and run your code again, to make sure it works for any input, not just the one on screen.

4. This spread tiering has a bug: a 720 bps credit comes out as "High yield" instead of "Distressed watch." Fix the order of the conditions.

id: m2-elif-order
title: Order matters
--- starter
spread_bps = 720

if spread_bps > 300:
    tier = "High yield"
elif spread_bps > 600:
    tier = "Distressed watch"
elif spread_bps > 1000:
    tier = "Distressed"
else:
    tier = "Investment grade"
--- tests
check(tier == "Distressed watch", f"720 bps should be 'Distressed watch' (yours: {tier!r})")
for value, expected in [(1200, "Distressed"), (400, "High yield"), (150, "Investment grade")]:
    ns = rerun("spread_bps = 720", f"spread_bps = {value}")
    check(ns["tier"] == expected, f"{value} bps should be {expected!r} (yours: {ns['tier']!r})")
--- hint
Python stops at the first true condition. 720 > 300 is true, so it never reaches the later tests.
--- hint
Put the highest threshold first: > 1000, then > 600, then > 300.

docs.text:
A credit has 2.0x leverage. Your code checks elif leverage <= 5.0 before leverage <= 3.0. Which bucket does it land in, and why?

Model answer

"Moderate." Python checks conditions top to bottom and stops at the first true one. 2.0 <= 5.0 is true, so it never reaches the <= 3.0 test. Put the narrowest condition first.

docs.title: 2.2 Functions
docs.text: Module 2 · about 40 minutes

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
So far, to price a second bond you'd copy the whole calculation and change the numbers. A function lets you write the calculation once and reuse it with any inputs, like a custom Excel formula (or Excel's LAMBDA).

def leverage(debt, ebitda):
    return debt / ebitda

print(leverage(450, 90))     # 5.0
print(leverage(350, 90))     # 3.888...
  • def starts a function definition. Next come its name, its parameters (the inputs) in parentheses, and a colon.
  • The indented body does the work. return hands the answer back to whoever called the function.
  • Calling it, as in leverage(450, 90), runs the body with debt = 450 and ebitda = 90. The values you pass in are the arguments.
  • Defining a function doesn't run it. Nothing happens until you call it.

return is not print. print shows a value on screen and then it's gone. return gives the value back so you can store it, compare it, or feed it into another calculation. A function with no return gives back None, Python's word for "nothing." It's the most common beginner bug, and exercise 3 below is about exactly that.

From here on, tests call your function with several different inputs, the way a model gets reused across deals.

docs.title: Explain it back
docs.text:
What's the difference between a function that ends with print(x) and one that ends with return x? When does it matter?

Model answer

print(x) only shows x on screen. The function still gives back None, so you can't store or reuse the result. return x hands x back to the caller, so you can save it in a variable, compare it, or pass it into another function. It matters any time the result feeds a later calculation, which in real work is almost always.

Next: 2.3 Decisions inside functions

docs.title: 2.3 Decisions inside functions
docs.text: Module 2 · about 40 minutes

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
Put if inside a function and the function can give different answers for different inputs, the way a pricing grid or a covenant does. A few patterns come up constantly.

Return a comparison directly. No if needed when the answer is just True/False:

def is_breach(leverage, max_leverage):
    return leverage > max_leverage

Return from inside each branch. return ends the function immediately, so the first branch that returns wins:

def spread_for(leverage):
    if leverage > 5.0:
        return 650
    elif leverage > 4.0:
        return 575
    return 500          # reached only if neither branch returned

Default values. def ear(nominal, periods_per_year=12) makes the second input optional. ear(0.12) uses 12, and ear(0.12, 4) overrides it. Parameters with defaults go last.

None for "no meaningful answer." Leverage with zero EBITDA, or a terminal value where WACC ≤ g, shouldn't produce a number or a crash. Return None and check for it with is None:

def safe_divide(a, b):
    if b == 0:
        return None
    return a / b

Good functions handle the edge cases an analyst would flag: zero, negative, exactly on the boundary, data in the wrong units. The tests below check those.

    return principal * r / (1 - (1 + r) ** -n)

docs.title: Explain it back
docs.text:
Why return None instead of 0 when EBITDA is zero and someone asks for leverage?

Model answer

Zero would be a wrong answer that looks like a great one: 0.0x leverage reads as no debt. None says "this has no meaningful value," and the code that uses it can check is None and flag it as N/M, the way a credit memo would, instead of quietly treating the credit as unlevered.

docs.title: 2.4 Building with functions
docs.text: Module 2 · about 35 minutes

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
Real tools are built from small functions that call each other, the way a model's summary tab pulls from the operating build, which pulls from the assumptions.

def ebitda(revenue, margin):
    return revenue * margin

def leverage(debt, revenue, margin):
    return debt / ebitda(revenue, margin)     # reuses ebitda()

Build and test each small piece on its own, then combine them. When something breaks, you'll know which piece to look at.

Scope. Variables created inside a function exist only inside it. They're its scratch work. Once the function returns, they're gone, and code outside can't see them. The only thing that leaves a function is what it returns. (If you try to use one of those variables outside, you'll get a NameError. Exercise 2 is exactly that bug.)

Returning two values. Separate them with a comma, then "unpack" them into two names when you call the function:

def mid_and_spread(bid, ask):
    mid = (bid + ask) / 2
    return mid, ask - bid

mid, width = mid_and_spread(99.5, 100.5)    # mid = 100.0, width = 1.0

Docstrings. A string on the first line of a function says what it does. Python ignores it, but your future self won't:

def leverage(debt, revenue, margin):
    """Total debt / EBITDA, in turns (x)."""

docs.title: 2.5 Capstone - covenant tool
docs.text: Module 2 · about 40 minutes

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
Nothing new here. You'll build a small covenant compliance tool out of three functions, each building on the last:

  1. covenant_test says PASS or BREACH, and gives headroom in turns.
  2. ebitda_cushion gives how far EBITDA can fall before a breach.
  3. covenant_line produces the one-line summary you'd paste into a portfolio monitoring report.

Definitions used here:

  • Leverage = debt / EBITDA.
  • Headroom (x) = max leverage - actual leverage. Negative means the borrower is already in breach.
  • EBITDA cushion = 1 - (debt / max leverage) / EBITDA. That's the share of EBITDA that can disappear before leverage hits the maximum, since debt / max leverage is the lowest EBITDA that still complies. Negative means EBITDA would have to grow to cure the breach.
  • If EBITDA is zero or negative, leverage isn't meaningful. Report it as N/M (not meaningful), as a credit memo would.

Each exercise below copies in the finished functions from the earlier steps, so every editor runs on its own.

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
1. Write covenant_test(debt, ebitda, max_lev). It returns two values, status and headroom:

  • EBITDA ≤ 0 gives ("N/M", None).
  • Leverage at or below the maximum gives "PASS", and above it gives "BREACH".
  • headroom is max_lev - leverage, where leverage = debt / EBITDA.
id: m2-cap-covenant
title: covenant_test
--- starter
def covenant_test(debt, ebitda, max_lev):
    """Return (status, headroom in turns) for a max leverage covenant."""

--- tests
status, headroom = covenant_test(450, 90, 5.25)
check(status == "PASS" and approx(headroom, 0.25), f"(450, 90, 5.25) should give ('PASS', 0.25) (yours: {status!r}, {headroom})")
status, headroom = covenant_test(500, 90, 5.25)
check(status == "BREACH" and approx(headroom, -0.3056, 0.001), f"(500, 90, 5.25) should give ('BREACH', about -0.31) (yours: {status!r}, {headroom})")
status, headroom = covenant_test(472.5, 90, 5.25)
check(status == "PASS", "exactly at 5.25x is a PASS")
check(covenant_test(100, 0, 5.0) == ("N/M", None), "zero EBITDA should give ('N/M', None)")
check(covenant_test(100, -5, 5.0) == ("N/M", None), "negative EBITDA should give ('N/M', None)")
--- hint
Handle the N/M case first: if ebitda <= 0: return "N/M", None
--- hint
Then leverage = debt / ebitda, headroom = max_lev - leverage, and an if/else for the status.
--- solution
def covenant_test(debt, ebitda, max_lev):
    """Return (status, headroom in turns) for a max leverage covenant."""
    if ebitda <= 0:
        return "N/M", None
    leverage = debt / ebitda
    headroom = max_lev - leverage
    if leverage <= max_lev:
        return "PASS", headroom
    return "BREACH", headroom

2. Write ebitda_cushion(debt, ebitda, max_lev): return the EBITDA cushion as a decimal, or None when EBITDA ≤ 0. The cushion is how far EBITDA can fall before the covenant breaks: minimum EBITDA = debt / max_lev, and cushion = 1 - minimum EBITDA / EBITDA.

id: m2-cap-cushion
title: ebitda_cushion
--- starter
def ebitda_cushion(debt, ebitda, max_lev):
    """Share of EBITDA that can be lost before breaching max leverage."""

--- tests
check(approx(ebitda_cushion(450, 90, 5.25), 0.0476, 0.0001), f"(450, 90, 5.25) should be about 0.0476 (yours: {ebitda_cushion(450, 90, 5.25)})")
check(approx(ebitda_cushion(500, 90, 5.25), -0.0582, 0.0001), "(500, 90, 5.25) should be about -0.0582: already in breach")
check(approx(ebitda_cushion(0, 90, 5.25), 1.0, 1e-9), "with no debt, all of EBITDA can go: the cushion is 1.0")
check(ebitda_cushion(100, 0, 5.0) is None, "zero EBITDA should give None")
--- hint
Handle EBITDA ≤ 0 first and return None. Then work out the minimum EBITDA, then the cushion.
--- solution
def ebitda_cushion(debt, ebitda, max_lev):
    """Share of EBITDA that can be lost before breaching max leverage."""
    if ebitda <= 0:
        return None
    min_ebitda = debt / max_lev
    return 1 - min_ebitda / ebitda

3. Write covenant_line(name, debt, ebitda, max_lev). It must call both functions above and return one of these formats:

Cedar Corp: PASS | 5.00x vs 5.25x max | 0.25x headroom | EBITDA cushion 4.8%
Birch Inc: BREACH | 5.56x vs 5.25x max | -0.31x headroom | EBITDA cushion -5.8%
Fir LLC: N/M | EBITDA not positive

id: m2-cap-line
title: covenant_line report
--- starter
def covenant_test(debt, ebitda, max_lev):
    if ebitda <= 0:
        return "N/M", None
    leverage = debt / ebitda
    headroom = max_lev - leverage
    if leverage <= max_lev:
        return "PASS", headroom
    return "BREACH", headroom


def ebitda_cushion(debt, ebitda, max_lev):
    if ebitda <= 0:
        return None
    return 1 - (debt / max_lev) / ebitda


def covenant_line(name, debt, ebitda, max_lev):
    """One-line covenant summary for a monitoring report."""

--- tests
line = covenant_line("Cedar Corp", 450, 90, 5.25)
check(line == "Cedar Corp: PASS | 5.00x vs 5.25x max | 0.25x headroom | EBITDA cushion 4.8%", f"Cedar Corp line is off. Yours: {line!r}")
line = covenant_line("Birch Inc", 500, 90, 5.25)
check(line == "Birch Inc: BREACH | 5.56x vs 5.25x max | -0.31x headroom | EBITDA cushion -5.8%", f"Birch Inc line is off. Yours: {line!r}")
line = covenant_line("Fir LLC", 100, 0, 5.0)
check(line == "Fir LLC: N/M | EBITDA not positive", f"Fir LLC line is off. Yours: {line!r}")
body = code.split("def covenant_line")[-1]
check("covenant_test(" in body and "ebitda_cushion(" in body, "covenant_line should call covenant_test(...) and ebitda_cushion(...)")
--- hint
Start with status, headroom = covenant_test(debt, ebitda, max_lev), and handle "N/M" first.
--- hint
Leverage for display is debt / ebitda with format .2f. Headroom uses .2f too, and the cushion uses .1%.
--- solution
def covenant_test(debt, ebitda, max_lev):
    if ebitda <= 0:
        return "N/M", None
    leverage = debt / ebitda
    headroom = max_lev - leverage
    if leverage <= max_lev:
        return "PASS", headroom
    return "BREACH", headroom


def ebitda_cushion(debt, ebitda, max_lev):
    if ebitda <= 0:
        return None
    return 1 - (debt / max_lev) / ebitda


def covenant_line(name, debt, ebitda, max_lev):
    """One-line covenant summary for a monitoring report."""
    status, headroom = covenant_test(debt, ebitda, max_lev)
    if status == "N/M":
        return f"{name}: N/M | EBITDA not positive"
    leverage = debt / ebitda
    cushion = ebitda_cushion(debt, ebitda, max_lev)
    return (f"{name}: {status} | {leverage:.2f}x vs {max_lev:.2f}x max | "
            f"{headroom:.2f}x headroom | EBITDA cushion {cushion:.1%}")

Once all three pass, add three more print(covenant_line(...)) calls for borrowers you make up. In Module 3 you'll run this over a whole portfolio with a loop instead of one line per borrower.

docs.title: Explain it back
docs.text:
Why does covenant_line call covenant_test instead of working out PASS/BREACH again itself?

Model answer

The rule lives in one place. If the covenant definition changes, say a step-down to 4.75x or a different EBITDA definition, you fix covenant_test once and every report that uses it updates. Copying the logic into each function is how two numbers in the same report end up disagreeing.

docs.text:
Module 2 · about 25 minutes

No hints, and the solution unlocks only after you pass. Write both from a blank editor.

1. DSCR test. Write dscr_status(cfads, debt_service). It returns:

  • "N/M" if debt service is zero or negative
  • "DEFAULT" if DSCR (cfads / debt_service) is below 1.00x
  • "LOCK-UP" if DSCR is at least 1.00x but below 1.15x (distributions blocked)
  • "OK" if DSCR is 1.15x or above
id: m2-cp-dscr
title: DSCR status
checkpoint: yes
--- starter

--- tests
for args, expected in [((120, 100), "OK"), ((115, 100), "OK"), ((110, 100), "LOCK-UP"),
                       ((100, 100), "LOCK-UP"), ((90, 100), "DEFAULT"), ((100, 0), "N/M"), ((100, -5), "N/M")]:
    check(dscr_status(*args) == expected, f"dscr_status{args} should be {expected!r} (yours: {dscr_status(*args)!r})")
--- solution
def dscr_status(cfads, debt_service):
    if debt_service <= 0:
        return "N/M"
    dscr = cfads / debt_service
    if dscr < 1.0:
        return "DEFAULT"
    elif dscr < 1.15:
        return "LOCK-UP"
    return "OK"

2. Rate-shock report. Write price_after_shock(price, duration, shock_bps), which uses the duration approximation: new price = price × (1 - duration × shock_bps / 10,000). Then write shock_report(price, duration). It must call price_after_shock and return exactly this format (shown for price 100, duration 6.5):

+100bp: $93.50 | -100bp: $106.50

id: m2-cp-shock
title: Rate-shock report
checkpoint: yes
--- starter

--- tests

check(approx(price_after_shock(100, 6.5, -100), 106.5), "price_after_shock(100, 6.5, -100) should be 106.5")

check("price_after_shock(" in code.split("def shock_report")[-1], "shock_report should call price_after_shock(...)")
--- solution
def price_after_shock(price, duration, shock_bps):
    return price * (1 - duration * shock_bps / 10000)


def shock_report(price, duration):
    up = price_after_shock(price, duration, 100)
    down = price_after_shock(price, duration, -100)
    return f"+100bp: ${up:,.2f} | -100bp: ${down:,.2f}"

docs.title: 3.1 Lists
docs.text: Module 3 · about 35 minutes

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
A list holds many values in order, like a row of cash flows or a column of prices. Use square brackets with commas between the items:

cash_flows = [-1000, 300, 400, 500, 200]

Positions start at 0, not 1. cash_flows[0] is the first item (-1000), and cash_flows[1] is the second. Think of the position as "how many steps from the start": year 0 is the investment, year 1 is the first inflow. Negative positions count from the end, so cash_flows[-1] is the last item (200).

You want Python Result Number of items len(cash_flows) 5 Total, smallest, largest sum(...), min(...), max(...) 400, -1000, 500 A slice: positions 1 up to (not including) 3 cash_flows[1:3] [300, 400] Everything from position 1 on cash_flows[1:] [300, 400, 500, 200] The last 2 cash_flows[-2:] [500, 200] Add to the end cash_flows.append(150) the list grows by one Is it in there? 500 in cash_flows True

Slices stop before the second number. [1:3] means positions 1 and 2. It feels odd at first, but it means [:3] is "the first 3" and [3:] is "everything after them," with no overlap.

Ask for a position that doesn't exist, like cash_flows[5] on a 5-item list, and you'll get a new error: IndexError.

docs.title: Explain it back
docs.text:
Why is year 1's cash flow at cash_flows[1], and why is that handy for finance?

Model answer

Positions start at 0, so the first item, the year-0 investment, is at position 0. Each year's cash flow then sits at the position equal to its year number, which means the position can serve directly as the discount exponent: cash_flows[t] / (1 + r) ** t.

Next: 3.2 For loops

docs.title: 3.2 For loops
docs.text: Module 3 · about 40 minutes

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
A for loop runs the same block once for every item in a list. It's the equivalent of dragging a formula down a column.

for cf in cash_flows:
    print(cf)

Read it as "for each cf in cash_flows, do the indented block." On each pass, cf holds the next item. The loop name (cf) is yours to choose. Pick one that reads well.

The running total is the pattern you'll use most. Start at zero before the loop, then add to it inside the loop:

total = 0
for cf in cash_flows:
    if cf > 0:
        total += cf        # += is shorthand for total = total + cf

Building a new list. Start with an empty list [] and .append inside the loop.

range for counting. range(5) gives 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, and range(1, 5) gives 1, 2, 3, 4. The end is excluded, like slices. Use it when you need the position, for example to compare each price with the one before it:

for i in range(1, len(prices)):
    daily_return = prices[i] / prices[i - 1] - 1

enumerate gives both the position and the item, which is exactly what discounting needs:

for t, cf in enumerate(cash_flows):     # t = 0, 1, 2, ...
    pv_total += cf / (1 + rate) ** t

def growth_path(start, rate, years):

    balance = start
    for year in range(years):

        path.append(balance)
    return path

docs.title: Explain it back
docs.text:
In daily_returns, why does the loop use range(1, len(prices)) instead of range(len(prices))?

Model answer

Each return compares prices[i] with prices[i - 1]. Starting at 0 would make the first comparison prices[0] vs prices[-1], which is the last price, giving a garbage return. Starting at 1 means the day before always exists, so n prices give n - 1 returns.

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
A dictionary (dict) is a lookup table. It maps keys to values, like a two-column range you'd VLOOKUP against. Use curly braces, with a colon between each key and its value:

prices = {"ACME": 120.5, "BRKN": 44.1, "CNDL": 312.0}
You want Python Look up a value prices["ACME"] gives 120.5 Add or update an entry prices["DLTA"] = 78.25 (the same syntax does both) Look up without crashing if it's missing prices.get("ZZZZ") gives None, and prices.get("ZZZZ", 0) gives 0 Check whether a key exists "ACME" in prices Loop over the pairs for ticker, price in prices.items(): Number of entries len(prices)

Look up a key that isn't there with square brackets and you'll get KeyError, the dictionary version of #N/A. Keys are exact, so "acme" and "ACME" are different keys.

Counting with .get is a pattern worth memorizing:

counts = {}
for rating in ratings:
    counts[rating] = counts.get(rating, 0) + 1

The first time a rating appears, .get returns 0, so its count becomes 1. After that, the count goes up by 1 each time.

docs.title: Explain it back
docs.text:
When would you use prices.get(ticker, 0) instead of prices[ticker]?

Model answer

When a missing key is normal and has a sensible fallback, like counting (the first occurrence starts at 0) or a ticker with no position. Use prices[ticker] when the key must exist. Then a KeyError is useful: it tells you the data is incomplete instead of quietly using 0.

Next: 3.4 Tables as lists of dicts

docs.title: 3.4 Tables as lists of dicts
docs.text: Module 3 · about 40 minutes

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
A spreadsheet table is rows and columns. In plain Python, the natural shape is a list of dicts: one dict per row, with the column names as keys. Here's a small loan tape:

loans = [
    {"id": "L001", "sector": "Industrials", "balance": 8.9,  "spread": 650, "status": "Performing"},
    {"id": "L002", "sector": "Healthcare",  "balance": 22.6, "spread": 475, "status": "Watchlist"},
    {"id": "L003", "sector": "Industrials", "balance": 15.0, "spread": 525, "status": "Performing"},
]

loans[1]["balance"] reads row 2's balance. Looping over the list gives you one row at a time:

for loan in loans:
    print(loan["id"], loan["balance"])

Almost every question about a table is one of four loop patterns, all of which you've seen:

Question Pattern Excel cousin Total balance? Running total SUM Which loans are on watch? Loop + if + append Filter Weighted average spread? Two running totals, divided SUMPRODUCT / SUM Exposure by sector? Dict of running totals Pivot table / SUMIF

Module 5 introduces pandas, which does each of these in one line. Writing them by hand first is how you'll understand what pandas is doing, and how you'll catch it when the result looks wrong.

docs.title: Explain it back
docs.text:
The weighted average spread (538.72 bps) is different from the simple average of the five spreads (545 bps). Which one belongs in a portfolio report, and why?

Model answer

The weighted one. It reflects what the portfolio actually earns per dollar lent: the $31.2m loan at 575 bps should count far more than the $8.9m loan at 650 bps. The simple average treats every loan as the same size, which overstates the portfolio's spread here because the small loans happen to carry higher spreads.

Next: 3.5 While loops and loop control

docs.title: 3.5 While loops and loop control
docs.text: Module 3 · about 35 minutes

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
A for loop runs a known number of times: once per item. A while loop runs until a condition stops being true, which suits questions like "how many years until the debt is repaid?" where you don't know the count in advance.

balance = 1.0
years = 0
while balance < 2.0:          # keep going while this is true
    balance *= 1.07
    years += 1

The danger: if nothing inside the loop ever makes the condition false, it runs forever. Some loans never amortize, for example, because the sweep doesn't even cover the interest. Guard against that before you loop. If you do write a runaway loop here, the site stops it after 10 seconds and tells you.

Two controls work in both kinds of loop:

  • break exits the loop right away. Use it when you've found what you were looking for, like the first year a covenant breaks.
  • continue skips the rest of this pass and moves to the next item. Use it to skip bad data, like a missing price.

Inside a function, return also exits the loop, since it ends the whole function. That's often the cleanest way to say "found it."

1. Write years_to_double(rate). It returns how many whole years compounding at rate takes to reach at least twice the starting amount. Each year the balance grows to balance × (1 + rate). Return None if rate is zero or negative, since the loop would never end.

title: Years to double
--- starter
def years_to_double(rate):

--- tests

check(years_to_double(0.10) == 8, "years_to_double(0.10) should be 8")
check(years_to_double(0.02) == 36, "years_to_double(0.02) should be 36")

--- hint
Guard first: if rate <= 0: return None
--- hint
Then the loop from the example, with rate instead of 0.07, and return years.
--- solution
def years_to_double(rate):
    if rate <= 0:
        return None
    balance = 1.0
    years = 0
    while balance < 2.0:
        balance *= 1 + rate
        years += 1
    return years

    return None

4. Write years_to_repay(debt, annual_sweep, rate). Each year, debt grows by interest and then the sweep is paid: debt = debt * (1 + rate) - annual_sweep. def years_to_repay(debt, annual_sweep, rate):
    if debt > 0 and annual_sweep <= debt * rate:
        return None
    years = 0
    while debt > 0:
        debt = debt * (1 + rate) - annual_sweep
        years += 1
    return years

docs.title: Explain it back
docs.text:
In years_to_repay, what would happen without the guard, if someone passed a sweep of 5 on $100 of debt at 8%?

Model answer

Interest adds $8 a year, but only $5 gets paid, so debt grows every year and debt > 0 stays true forever. That's an infinite loop. The site would stop it after 10 seconds, but in a real script it would just hang. The guard spots the impossible case up front and returns None, the same "no meaningful answer" idea from Module 2.

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
This is the full schedule you'd build in Excel by dragging a row down 360 times. Each period:

interest   = beginning balance * periodic rate
principal  = payment - interest
ending     = beginning balance - principal
next period's beginning balance = this period's ending balance

Each row is a dict, and the schedule is a list of those dicts, the same shape as the loan tape in 3.4:

{"period": 1, "begin": 250000.0, "payment": 1580.17, "interest": 1354.17, "principal": 226.00, "end": 249774.00}

You'll build it in three steps: the schedule, a summary of it, then an early-paydown scenario that answers a question a borrower might ask: what does an extra $200 a month save?

Each starter includes the finished payment() function from Module 2.

def payment(principal, annual_rate, years, periods_per_year=12):

Why does exercise 1 use a for loop but exercise 3 a while loop?

def sector_weights(holdings):
    by_sector = {}
    total = 0
    for h in holdings:
        value = h["shares"] * h["price"]
        by_sector[h["sector"]] = by_sector.get(h["sector"], 0) + value
        total += value
    weights = {}
    for sector, value in by_sector.items():

    return weights

docs.title: 4.1 Handling errors
docs.text: Module 4 · about 35 minutes

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
So far an error has meant "fix your code." But some errors come from the data, not the code. A price of "N/A", a blank balance, a zero EBITDA. You can't fix the file, so you tell Python what to do when it happens. That's try / except, the cousin of Excel's IFERROR:

try:
    price = float(text)
except ValueError:
    price = None

Python runs the try block. If a ValueError happens anywhere inside it, Python jumps to the except block instead of crashing. If nothing goes wrong, the except block is skipped.

Catch specific errors. Name the error you expect, so you only swallow the problem you've planned for. The ones you'll catch most:

Error When it happens ValueError float("N/A"), int("1,000"): text that isn't a valid number ZeroDivisionError Dividing by zero KeyError A dict lookup for a key that isn't there TypeError Math on None, or text plus a number

You can list several: except (ZeroDivisionError, TypeError):. A bare except: with no error named catches everything, including your own typos, so avoid it.

raise your own errors. When a caller passes nonsense, like a loan with -5 years, stop with a clear message instead of returning a garbage number:

if years <= 0:
    raise ValueError("years must be positive")

It's a judgment call which to use. Return None when missing data is expected and the caller can carry on, like a blank row in a loan tape. Raise an error when the input means someone made a mistake that must be fixed.

--- solution
def annual_payment(principal, rate, years):
    if years <= 0:
        raise ValueError("years must be positive")
    if principal < 0:
        raise ValueError("principal can't be negative")
    if rate == 0:
        return principal / years
    return principal * rate / (1 - (1 + rate) ** -years)

docs.title: Explain it back
docs.text:
parse_money returns None for a blank balance, but annual_payment raises an error for negative years. Why treat them differently?

Model answer

A blank balance is a normal data problem. Real loan tapes have gaps, and the code reading them should flag the row and keep going. Negative years means whoever called the function made a mistake, so a number would be meaningless. Raising stops the program with a clear message, so the mistake gets fixed instead of a wrong payment flowing into a model.

docs.text: Module 4 · about 40 minutes

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
Real data lives in files. To read one, open it inside a with block. The file closes itself when the block ends, even if an error happens:

with open("trades.csv") as f:
    for line in f:
        print(line.strip())      # each line ends in a newline; strip removes it

The name "trades.csv" is a path. A bare file name means "in the current folder." On this site the practice files are already in place. On your laptop (4.3) the file needs to be in the same folder as your notebook.

A CSV is just text with commas, but splitting on commas yourself breaks on values like "1,000". Use the built-in csv module, which handles quoting correctly:

You want Python Rows as lists csv.reader(f) gives ["T0002", "2025-04-25", "CNDL", ...] per row The header row on its own header = next(reader). next takes the next row and moves past it Rows as dicts keyed by the header csv.DictReader(f) gives {"trade_id": "T0002", "ticker": "CNDL", ...} per row, the list-of-dicts shape from 3.4 Write a file open(path, "w", newline=""), then csv.writer(f).writerow([...])

Everything read from a CSV is text. "780" is a string until you convert it with int() or float(), which is where 4.1's error handling earns its keep.

Start a program that uses the module with import csv at the top. Importing loads one of Python's built-in toolkits. You'll import pandas the same way in Module 5.

docs.title: Explain it back
docs.text:
csv.DictReader gives you {"quantity": "780", ...}. Why can't you add up quantities straight away, and what could go wrong when you convert them?

Model answer

Every value from a CSV is text, so "780" has to go through int() before you can do math with it, and adding two strings just glues them together. The conversion fails on bad values like "N/A", blanks, or "1,000" (int can't read the comma), so each conversion needs cleaning and a try / except to deal with the rows that won't parse.

docs.title: 4.3 Python on your laptop
docs.text: Module 4 · about 30 minutes, once

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
The browser has been a sandbox. Real work, the CFA module included, happens in a Jupyter notebook on your own machine. A notebook is a document of cells: code cells you run one at a time, with the result shown directly underneath, and text cells for notes. Think of it as a model where every step's output is visible as you build.

You'll install three things, once:

Piece What it is Why you need it Python The language itself Runs your code VS Code A free code editor from Microsoft Opens notebooks, edits scripts, has a built-in terminal A virtual environment (.venv) A private folder of packages for one project Keeps pandas and friends from clashing across projects

These steps are for Windows. If something doesn't match what you see, check the troubleshooting table at the end.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
1. Check for Python, and install it if it's missing. Open the Start menu, type Terminal, and open it. Then run:

python --version

If it prints Python 3.12 or newer, skip to step 2. Otherwise, download the Windows installer from python.org/downloads. On its first screen, tick "Add python.exe to PATH", then choose Install Now. Close the terminal, open a new one, and run the version check again.

2. Install VS Code from code.visualstudio.com. Open it, click the Extensions icon in the left sidebar (four squares), and install Python and Jupyter. Both are published by Microsoft.

3. Make a project folder. Create a folder such as Documents\python-practice. In VS Code, choose File > Open Folder and pick it.

4. Create the virtual environment and install packages. In VS Code, open Terminal > New Terminal and run these two commands one at a time. The second takes a minute or two.

python -m venv .venv

.venv\Scripts\python -m pip install jupyter pandas matplotlib

The first creates a .venv folder inside your project. The second installs Jupyter, pandas and matplotlib into it, and nowhere else on your laptop.

5. Download the starter files into the project folder:

  • module-4-first-notebook.ipynb
  • trades.csv
  • loan_tape.csv

If a file opens in the browser instead of downloading, right-click the link and choose Save link as.

6. Open the notebook. Click module-4-first-notebook.ipynb in VS Code's file list. At the top right, click Select Kernel, then Python Environments, and pick the one marked .venv. The kernel is the Python that runs your cells, and choosing .venv means it can see the packages you just installed.

7. Work through the notebook. Click into the first code cell and press Shift+Enter to run it and move to the next. Section 4 asks you to paste in your parse_money from lesson 4.1. When everything passes, do the honest test in section 7: Restart, then Run All.

docs.title: How notebooks behave
docs.text:
• Order matters, not position. A cell can use any variable from a cell that has already run, wherever that cell sits on the page. Run cells out of order and the notebook can work today but break tomorrow. Restart and Run All catches that.
  • The last line displays itself. A bare debt / ebitda on the last line of a cell shows its value, with no print needed. pandas tables display nicely this way.
  • The number next to a cell, like [3], is the order cells ran in. Gaps or jumps in those numbers are a hint that the notebook was run out of order.
  • Scripts vs. notebooks. A .py file runs top to bottom in one go: run it with .venv\Scripts\python my_script.py. Use notebooks to explore and present, and scripts for anything you'll rerun the same way every time.

Your notebook runs fine now, but fails after Restart and Run All with NameError: name 'loans' is not defined. What happened?

Model answer

Somewhere a cell uses loans before the cell that creates it, either because it sits higher on the page or because the creating cell was deleted or edited. docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
A trade blotter, the list of trades a desk did, arrives as a CSV. Before you total anything, you need clean rows, and a record of every row you threw out and why. Silently dropping rows is how breaks go unexplained, and an operations or audit team will ask about each one.

trades.csv has 120 rows with three kinds of problems planted in it. Open it in Excel and look for them first:

  • Rows cut short, with missing fields
  • Prices of N/A
  • Side labels with stray case and spaces, like sell

Your loader will check each row in this order. The first problem found becomes the row's reason:

Check If it fails, the reason is The row has exactly 6 fields "missing fields" Side, after .strip().upper(), is BUY or SELL "bad side" Quantity, after removing commas, converts with int() "bad quantity" Price converts with float() "bad price"

Skip blank lines completely: they're not trades.

import csv


def load_trades(path):
    """Read a trade blotter. Return (clean trades, bad rows with a reason)."""
    clean = []
    bad = []
    with open(path) as f:
        reader = csv.reader(f)
        next(reader)                        # skip the header
        for row in reader:
            if not row:
                continue                    # blank line
            if len(row) != 6:
                bad.append({"trade_id": row[0], "reason": "missing fields"})
                continue
            trade_id, date, ticker, side, quantity, price = row
            side = side.strip().upper()
            if side not in ("BUY", "SELL"):
                bad.append({"trade_id": trade_id, "reason": "bad side"})
                continue
            try:
                quantity = int(quantity.replace(",", ""))
            except ValueError:
                bad.append({"trade_id": trade_id, "reason": "bad quantity"})
                continue
            try:
                price = float(price)
            except ValueError:
                bad.append({"trade_id": trade_id, "reason": "bad price"})
                continue
            clean.append({"trade_id": trade_id, "date": date, "ticker": ticker,
                          "side": side, "quantity": quantity, "price": price})
    return clean, bad

docs.title: Explain it back
docs.text:
Why does load_trades return the bad rows with a reason, instead of just skipping them?

Model answer

The totals are only trustworthy if you can account for every row: 110 clean plus 10 exceptions equals the 120 in the file. With a reason attached, operations can fix the source: chase the missing prices, rebook the truncated trades. Silent skipping makes notional quietly too low, and nobody can say why.

def parse_pct(text):
    cleaned = text.strip()
    is_percent = cleaned.endswith("%")
    if is_percent:
        cleaned = cleaned[:-1]
    try:
        value = float(cleaned)
    except ValueError:
        return None
    if is_percent:
        return value / 100
    return value

import csv

def total_clean_balance(path):

docs.title: 5.1 NumPy arrays
docs.text: Module 5 · about 55 minutes

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
A NumPy array is a list of numbers that does math on every item at once, with no loop. That's how Excel treats a whole column when you write one formula and fill it down:

import numpy as np

cash_flows = np.array([-1000, 300, 400, 500, 200])
years = np.arange(len(cash_flows))           # array([0, 1, 2, 3, 4])
factors = 1 / (1 + 0.10) ** years             # one discount factor per year
npv = (cash_flows * factors).sum()            # 115.57
  • import numpy as np loads NumPy under the short name np. Everyone uses that name.
  • Math between an array and a number applies to every item: prices * 2, 1 / (1 + r) ** years.
  • Math between two arrays of the same length works item by item: cash_flows * factors.
  • Arrays have methods: .sum(), .mean(), .max(), .min(), .std().
  • Slices work like lists: prices[1:] drops the first item and prices[:-1] drops the last. So prices[1:] / prices[:-1] - 1 gives every daily return at once.

Sample vs. population standard deviation. arr.std() divides by n by default (population). For volatility from a sample of returns, you want n - 1, the version you used in econometrics: arr.std(ddof=1). Annualize daily volatility by multiplying by √252, written np.sqrt(252).

Masks are arrays of True/False, and they're how you filter:

lev = np.array([4.2, 5.6, 3.1, 6.3])
over = lev > 5.25          # array([False, True, False, True])
lev[over]                   # array([5.6, 6.3])
over.sum()                  # 2. True counts as 1
np.where(over, "BREACH", "PASS")   # an IF() applied to the whole array

docs.title: Explain it back
docs.text:
Why does annualized volatility use ddof=1, and what would change if you left it out?

Model answer

Daily returns are a sample, not the whole population, so the unbiased variance divides by n - 1. That's what ddof=1 does ("delta degrees of freedom"). Without it NumPy divides by n, which slightly understates volatility. Over thousands of days the gap is tiny, but on short samples it matters, and the CFA material and Excel's STDEV.S both use the sample version.

docs.title: 5.2 DataFrames
docs.text: Module 5 · about 55 minutes

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
A pandas DataFrame is a table: named columns, numbered rows, and a type for each column. It replaces the list-of-dicts from 3.4 and the csv loops from 4.2:

import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("holdings.csv")       # the whole file, already typed
You want pandas What comes back First rows df.head() (or df.head(10)) A smaller DataFrame Rows and columns df.shape (20, 6) Column names df.columns.tolist() A list Column types df.dtypes int64, float64, or object (text) One column df["price"] A Series: one column with the row labels Several columns df[["ticker", "price"]] A DataFrame. Note the double brackets: a list inside [] A new column df["market_value"] = df["shares"] * df["price"] Computed for every row at once, like NumPy Column math df["price"].sum(), .mean(), .max(), .min() One number Quick stats df.describe() Count, mean, std and quartiles per numeric column A Series to a list df["ticker"].tolist() A Python list

A Series is a single column, and most column methods return one. Think of a DataFrame as a dict of Series that share the same row labels.

You can also build a DataFrame from a dict of lists, with keys as column names:

pd.DataFrame({"ticker": ["ACME", "BRKN"], "weight": [0.6, 0.4]})

print(df) shows the table as text. In a notebook, a bare df on the last line of a cell shows a formatted table.

Why did pandas read balance as text, and why does that matter before you sum it?

Model answer

docs.title: 5.3 Selecting and filtering
docs.text: Module 5 · about 55 minutes

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
Filtering in pandas uses the NumPy masks from 5.1. A comparison on a column gives a True/False Series, and putting that inside df[...] keeps the True rows. It's Excel's AutoFilter as code:

expensive = df[df["price"] > 100]

Combining conditions uses & (and), | (or) and ~ (not), not the words and / or. Put each condition in parentheses, because & binds tighter than >:

df[(df["sector"] == "Technology") & (df["price"] < 100)]

Forget the parentheses or use and, and you'll get a confusing ValueError: The truth value of a Series is ambiguous. That message almost always means one of those two mistakes.

You want pandas Rows where a column is one of several values df[df["sector"].isin(["Technology", "Energy"])] Rows and specific columns together df.loc[df["price"] > 100, ["ticker", "price"]] One column of the filtered rows, as a list df.loc[mask, "ticker"].tolist() Sort df.sort_values("market_value", ascending=False) The top N by a column df.nlargest(10, "market_value") Count the rows that match mask.sum() or len(df[mask])

.loc[rows, columns] reads as "these rows, these columns." The rows can be a mask, and the columns a name or a list of names.

docs.title: Explain it back
docs.text:
df[df["sector"] == "Energy" & df["price"] < 100] raises an error. What two fixes might it need, and why?

Model answer

It needs parentheses around each condition. Without them, Python evaluates "Energy" & df["price"] first, because & binds tighter than == and <, which is nonsense. Also, & must be used rather than and: and asks for a single True/False, and a whole column of them is "ambiguous." The fixed version: df[(df["sector"] == "Energy") & (df["price"] < 100)].

Next: 5.4 Grouping and reshaping

docs.title: 5.4 Grouping and reshaping
docs.text: Module 5 · about 60 minutes

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
groupby is a pivot table. It splits the rows into groups, applies a calculation to each group, and combines the results. Read it left to right as "by sector, take market value, sum it":

df.groupby("sector")["market_value"].sum()

The result is a Series with one row per sector, and the sector names become the row labels (the index). That's the exposure_by_sector loop from 3.4, in one line.

You want pandas One statistic per group df.groupby("sector")["market_value"].sum() (or .mean(), .count(), .max()) Several statistics, named df.groupby("sector").agg(positions=("ticker", "count"), mv=("market_value", "sum")) Count rows per value df["sector"].value_counts() A Series to a dict .to_dict() Sort a result .sort_values(ascending=False) The group labels back as a normal column .reset_index()

Weighted averages by group: build the weighted column first, then divide the group sums: sum(balance × spread) / sum(balance). It's the same formula as 3.4, but applied per group.

Reshaping: long vs. wide. prices.csv is long: one row per date and ticker. Analysis usually wants it wide: one row per date and one column per ticker, like a price sheet in Excel. pivot does that:

wide = prices.pivot(index="date", columns="ticker", values="close")

Once it's wide, wide["ACME"] is a single ticker's price history, and wide.pct_change() gives every ticker's daily returns at once. That's Module 7's starting point.

docs.title: 5.5 Capstone - portfolio holdings
docs.text: Module 5 · about 60 minutes

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
This is the holdings page of a portfolio review, built in pandas: what you own, what it's worth, where the money sits, and whether any position breaks a concentration limit. Four functions:

  1. enrich(df) adds market value, cost, unrealized P&L, P&L % and portfolio weight.
  2. sector_exposure(df) gives each sector's weight, largest first.
  3. top_n_share(df, n) and hhi(df) measure concentration.
  4. over_limit(df, limit) lists the positions above a single-name limit.

Two concentration measures:

  • Top-N share: the weight held in the N largest positions. "The top 10 are 79% of the book" is a sentence every PM and risk committee recognizes.
  • HHI (Herfindahl-Hirschman Index): the sum of the squared weights. It ranges from 1/N (perfectly equal) to 1 (everything in one name). Its inverse, 1 / HHI, is the effective number of positions: how many equal-sized holdings would give the same concentration. Credit and antitrust analysts use the same measure.

Each starter after the first includes a finished enrich.

Model answer

The portfolio behaves like 12 equal-sized positions, not 20. A handful of large names (VMLT alone is about 15.6%) carry most of the risk, and the small positions add little diversification. import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def ann_vol_by_ticker(path):
    prices = pd.read_csv(path)
    wide = prices.pivot(index="date", columns="ticker", values="close")
    returns = wide.pct_change().dropna()
    vol = returns.std() * np.sqrt(252)
    return vol.sort_values(ascending=False)

import pandas as pd

def pnl_by_sector(path):
    df = pd.read_csv(path)
    df["unrealized_pnl"] = df["shares"] * (df["price"] - df["cost_basis"])
    return df.groupby("sector")["unrealized_pnl"].sum().sort_values(ascending=False)
